newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK - 30-year then relief.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKETS OUTLOOK - 30-year then relief.

text.p: U.S. credit markets have already targeted potent economic releases next week but players must first contend with the third and final leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding, analysts said.

While experts believe fixed-income markets will retain a favorable tone, they also believe the government's sale of $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Wednesday afternoon may pose a barrier to achieving new highs for the markets.
The Treasury sold $10.0 billion 10-year notes on Wednesday at an average yield of 6.273 percent, as expected.

Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said the markets should be looking for some concession for Treasuries after watching three- and 10-year auctions bid at high levels.
"(Dealers) don't want to bid again at the highs, there's just nothing to hang your hat on," Rupkey said.
Rupkey said the 30-year bond yield may hit 6-5/8 percent.

But the fact the auctions have not thrown the markets into disarray after being bid near highs is encouraging for the big picture, said Lee Youngdahl, vice president and economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.
"It's assumed that there's a bid under the market for this paper," Youngdahl said. Reflecting that, he noted dealers passed on an opportunity to sell three-year T-notes at a profit Tuesday night.
At the same time, Youngdahl expects some near-term indigestion will persist into next week. Dealers will test the bid given the recent absence of upside impetus, he said.

Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, contended upward momentum for governments will continue once the effects of the refunding wear off. That investor sentiment is already exhibited in equities, he said.
"The rally has stalled and that is primarily due to the auctions," Johnson said. "Investor sentiment is strong, look at the stock market, and that should also help bonds."

Technically speaking, Rupkey said the backup from overnight highs may suggest the market have visited best levels for the near-term. The long-term outlook is still up, he said, but supply is likely to choke the market now.

"The highs (achieved) in Tokyo are leaving a nasty skid mark on the charts," he said. "It's a higher high and now we're closing lower on the day and some people take that, technically, to mean a top."
Looking at economic data, Lanston's Youngdahl said none of the numbers should be too earth-shattering.
"Typically productivity is not a big market mover, nor is consumer credit," he said, adding the initial claims data could be thrown awry by the General Motors strike.

In a Reuters poll, economists forecast jobless claims rose 2,000 in the week ended November 2. The average forecast for third quarter productivity calls for a 0.1 percent slide compared to the second quarter's 0.5 percent gain.

The government is slated to release first time jobless claims data on Thursday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Productivity figures are due out at 1000 EST/1500 GMT and consumer credit data for September caps the day at 1500 EST/2000 GMT.

Johnson said productivity may not move the markets but the markets will watch to see if rises there offset higher wages. He expects that not to happen, however, with a forecast for a flat third quarter read.
Data next week, including the producer and consumer price indeces, is expected to be benign, Youngdahl said.
The Fed Funds is expected to open on Thursday between 5d-1/4 percent and 5-5/16 percent.
